title: All mine is with me
hook: Stilpo lost city, wife and children and said everything of his was still with him

segments.voice: Yesterday: an audience of one. Your line was one is enough. Did you do one piece of good work for one person, without counting who noticed? Day four hundred forty-three.

A city has just fallen. The conqueror, a king called Demetrius, nicknamed the Besieger of Cities, has taken Megara. Houses are wrecked, goods carried off, families scattered. Somewhere in the ruins stands a philosopher named Stilpo, whose home is gone and whose wife and children are lost to him. The king asks him: have you lost anything? Seneca tells the story, and Stilpo's answer, in his ninth letter. Today: all mine is with me.
screen: `MEGARA HAS FALLEN.` → `HAVE YOU LOST ANYTHING?` → `ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

segments.voice: First, the answer. Stilpo told the king: I have all my goods with me. Seneca explains what he meant. Stilpo had his true goods with him, the kind no hand can seize. What was scattered, wrecked and carried off, he did not count as his own, only as things that had come to him from outside. Second, the hard part. It's fair to flinch at this story. Losing a family is not a small thing, and Seneca doesn't say it is. In the same letter he says the wise person feels their troubles, and then overcomes them. Not numb. Not untouched. Still standing. Third, the friendship twist. The surprising thing is where Seneca puts this story: in a letter about friendship. Lucilius has asked whether a person who is complete in themselves needs friends at all. Seneca says the wise person is content with themselves, and can live without friends if they must, but still wants them, very much. Not to have someone who'll sit at their bedside, but to have someone at whose bedside they can sit. Fourth, the balance. So Stilpo's line isn't a reason to love less. Read this way, it's a reason to love without fear. If what's most yours can't be taken, you can give your heart to people and things freely, knowing that even if you lose them, you won't lose yourself. In Seneca's Latin: omnia mea mecum sunt. All mine is with me.
screen: `I HAVE ALL MY GOODS WITH ME.` · `FEELING IT, AND STILL STANDING.` · `WANTING FRIENDS ANYWAY.` · `LOVE WITHOUT FEAR.` · then, large: `ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Take something to write on, or just count on your fingers. List a few things that are yours in Stilpo's sense, things no fire, thief or bad day could take from you. Your honesty. Your patience, on good days. The way you keep a promise. What you've learned. The love you give, even if it isn't returned. Name three, slowly. Then hold your hands together in your lap, as if holding them, and breathe. All of this is with you, right now. The bell holds the time.
All mine is with me. Stilpo's answer after losing his city: his true goods, the kind no hand can seize, were still with him. Seneca's ninth letter. Today's word.
screen: `ALL MINE IS WITH ME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: all mine is with me. Keep your short list with you today. When something goes missing, a plan, a thing, a chance, touch the list once. Day four hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism reflect on which of their goods are truly their own, character, judgment, kindness, so that losses elsewhere do not take away their footing.

fork.reveal: he said his goods were all with him: not the city or the house, but the true goods no hand can seize.

original.note: Latin: all mine is with me, Stilpo's answer as Seneca tells it.

trapdoor: what it means: Stilpo counted only the goods no one could seize as truly his, so losing his city could not take what was most his own.
what a scholar hears: Seneca says Stilpo counted what was plundered not as his own but as things that had come from outside; Cicero tells a similar saying of Bias of Priene.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the list 'justice, courage, good sense' comes from De Constantia 5.6, not Letter 9; teach, word, match, fork and trapdoor now follow Letter 9.18–19 (true goods no hand can seize; what was plundered counted as from outside). Cut 'two thousand years', 'stuck for centuries as a proverb', 'old', 'smoke' and the proverb myth.

Letter 9.18–19: Demetrius Poliorcetes takes Megara; Stilpo, having lost his children and wife, answers 'omnia mea mecum sunt'; Seneca glosses his goods as justice, virtue, temperance, prudence. Paraphrased; confirm the list of virtues.
Letter 9.3: the wise man 'feels' his troubles but overcomes them; 9.8: the wise man wants a friend in order to have someone by whose sickbed he can sit. Paraphrased; confirm.
Whether Stilpo's family were killed or captured is not specified by Seneca ('lost'); the script keeps 'lost to him'.
Zeno studying with Stilpo (Diogenes Laertius 7.2, 7.24) and Cicero's 'omnia mecum porto mea' attributed to Bias (Paradoxa Stoicorum 1.8): confirm.
